description: A pathway based on the experimentally investigated cyanosulfidic chemistry of Patel et al. (2015). Simple feedstocks are converted through acrylonitrile, aminopropanal, hydroxythioamides, and a cyclic thiolactam into a proline aminonitrile. Subsequent hydrolysis yields racemic proline. Obtaining specifically L-Proline requires an additional, hypothetical enantioenrichment or resolution process.
scientific_status: Experimentally supported synthesis of a proline precursor, followed by chemically plausible hydrolysis and a hypothetical prebiotic chiral-resolution step.

molecules.role: Prebiotic sulfur reagent and photochemical reductant

reactions.name: Formation of acrylonitrile
reactions.conditions: Cu(I)-based catalysis in a proposed prebiotic setting
reactions.description: Acetylene reacts with hydrogen cyanide to generate acrylonitrile, a three-carbon precursor.
reactions.evidence: Known chemical transformation incorporated into the proposed prebiotic scenario.

reactions.name: Ammonia addition to acrylonitrile
reactions.description: Ammonia adds across the carbon-carbon double bond, producing beta-aminopropionitrile.
reactions.evidence: Experimentally demonstrated in the cited prebiotic chemistry.

reactions.name: Photoreduction to aminopropanal
reactions.conditions: UV irradiation, aqueous hydrogen sulfide or hydrosulfide; copper photoredox chemistry may assist
reactions.description: The nitrile functional group is reduced to an aldehyde, generating 3-aminopropanal. Water participates in the overall conversion.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin formation
reactions.description: Hydrogen cyanide adds to the aldehyde, extending the carbon skeleton from three to four carbon atoms.

reactions.name: Formation of open-chain hydroxythioamide
reactions.description: The nitrile is transformed into a thioamide through reaction with reduced sulfur.
reactions.evidence: Experimentally observed as one product of the reaction.

reactions.name: Alternative cyclic hydroxythioamide formation
reactions.description: A competing branch forms the five-membered cyclic alpha-hydroxythioamide. This is an alternative product of step 5, not an additional required linear step.

reactions.name: Reductive cyclization to gamma-butyrothiolactam
reactions.conditions: UV irradiation, hydrogen sulfide or hydrosulfide
reactions.description: The open-chain hydroxythioamide undergoes reductive deoxygenation and cyclization, forming a five-membered sulfur-containing ring.
reactions.evidence: Experimentally supported; the open-chain and cyclic hydroxythioamide mixture gives the thiolactam.

reactions.name: Deoxygenation of cyclic hydroxythioamide
reactions.conditions: UV irradiation, hydrogen sulfide or hydrosulfide
reactions.description: The alternative cyclic intermediate also converges on gamma-butyrothiolactam.
reactions.evidence: Experimentally supported as part of the observed hydroxythioamide mixture conversion.

reactions.name: Reduction of thiolactam to pyrroline
reactions.conditions: UV irradiation, hydrogen sulfide or hydrosulfide
reactions.description: The cyclic thioamide is photoreduced to a cyclic imine. The cyclic imine is the chemically relevant intermediate for the subsequent cyanide addition.
reactions.evidence: Supported by the experimentally investigated conversion of gamma-butyrothiolactam to the proline aminonitrile.

reactions.name: Formation of proline aminonitrile
reactions.description: Cyanide adds to the carbon of the cyclic imine, producing 2-cyanopyrrolidine. The new stereocenter forms without inherent L-selectivity.
reactions.evidence: Experimentally demonstrated as part of the two-step thiolactam-to-aminonitrile sequence.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of proline aminonitrile
reactions.conditions: Aqueous hydrolysis; sufficient thermal or acid/base activation
reactions.description: Hydrolysis converts the nitrile group into a carboxylic acid, yielding DL-Proline. This is a chemically established class of transformation, but the complete prebiotic hydrolysis of this particular precursor was not demonstrated in the cited 2015 pathway.
reactions.evidence: Chemically plausible extension of the experimentally demonstrated aminonitrile synthesis.

reactions.name: Enantiomeric resolution to obtain L-Proline
reactions.conditions: Hypothetical prebiotic chiral selection or enantioenrichment followed by separation
reactions.description: Racemic proline contains L- and D-Proline. Obtaining an L-enriched fraction requires a symmetry-breaking process, such as a pre-existing small L-enantiomeric excess and an appropriate selective crystallization or partitioning mechanism. This step separates enantiomers; it does not convert every D-Proline molecule into L-Proline.
reactions.evidence: Proline enantioenrichment has experimental precedents under particular crystallization and solvent conditions, but a fully demonstrated early-Earth-compatible process producing enantiopure L-Proline is not established.

prebiotic_environment.setting: Hypothetical anoxic early-Earth surface pools or streams associated with impact-generated feedstocks and mineral deposits
important_assumptions: A source of acetylene and concentrated cyanide is available.
Relevant feedstocks encounter one another in the appropriate sequence.
Reductive sulfur photochemistry operates under suitable aqueous conditions.
Hydrolysis of the proline aminonitrile can occur without excessive decomposition.
An additional asymmetric process is necessary to obtain specifically L-Proline.

limitations: The 2015 experiments established a pathway to the aminonitrile precursor of proline, not a complete demonstrated synthesis of enantiopure L-Proline.
The indicated conversions involve distinct chemical environments and should not be interpreted as a validated single-pot prebiotic synthesis.
The network represents major organic transformations; photochemical electron donors, oxidized sulfur byproducts, and all acid-base equilibria are not fully enumerated.
Without a chiral influence, proline synthesis produces both enantiomers rather than exclusively L-Proline.
The proposed chiral-resolution step is not demonstrated to have operated on early Earth.
